Examples of third-party clients and technologies. Configure them separately; coexistence depends on routes and DNS. A client in TUN mode takes over routes; in proxy mode, only configured apps use it.

This example assumes no route or DNS conflicts. ocbar manages one session of its own; configure the personal VPN separately. Routes are selected by network or destination address, not by application.

01 / Routes

Work VPN.
Within your boundaries.

Choose the networks that need the work tunnel in ocbar. Your personal internet and home devices keep their own routes.

Work range 10.20.0.0/16 is selected. Personal VPN and LAN keep separate routes.

A schematic comparison of configurations. Full tunnel here means a profile that sends internet traffic through the VPN; LAN access depends on the profile routes.

02 / Names and addresses

Resolve first.
Then connect.

Split DNS sends queries for work names to the corporate DNS server. Public names use your usual resolver. Routes determine where the actual traffic goes.

03 / In your menu bar

Routes on the map.
Control at hand.

Profiles, connection controls and logs in your macOS menu bar. Network settings live in the profile editor. Actual ocbar screenshots with demonstration data.

Share a profile

A .ocbar file carries connection settings. Each colleague signs in with their own account.

Your own CSD wrapper

Provide your own wrapper for environment checks. The gateway decides whether to grant access.

Local SOCKS

With ocproxy and SystemProxy=off: no root, system routes or DNS changes. Configure your app to use SOCKS separately.

Open on the inside.

Source code is available under MIT. Inspect how connections, routes and DNS work, and use logs to understand a particular session.
